title: Molecular Genetic Analysis of the Rabies Virus in Wild and Domestic Animals of Kazakhstan and the Development of a Diagnostic System

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies remains one of the most significant zoonotic infections, characterized by high mortality.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In Kazakhstan, the virus circulates among both domestic and wild animals, necessitating ongoing molecular genetic monitoring and improved laboratory diagnostic methods.
analysis.methods: The aim of this study was to investigate the genetic characteristics of the rabies virus circulating among animals in Kazakhstan using nucleoprotein (N) gene analysis and to develop a regionally adapted real-time RT-PCR method for its detection.
analysis.main_results: Kazakhstani rabies virus isolates deposited in GenBank revealed that all belong to a cosmopolitan lineage and form a single phylogenetic cluster, regardless of host species.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The obtained data were used to develop a real-time PCR method based on the genetic characteristics of the rabies virus circulating in Kazakhstan.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The proposed method ensures reliable detection of rabies virus variants circulating in Kazakhstan and can be used for laboratory diagnostics and epidemiological monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The diagnostic performance of the method was evaluated using 144 samples of various origins obtained from domestic and wild animals, including bats.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to investigate the genetic characteristics of the rabies virus circulating among animals in Kazakhstan and develop a regionally adapted real-time RT-PCR method for its detection. The research found that all Kazakhstani rabies virus isolates belong to a cosmopolitan lineage and form a single phylogenetic cluster, regardless of host species. The study included isolates from neighboring countries, such as China and Russia, to demonstrate the regional relationship of circulating virus variants. The developed assay demonstrated a sensitivity of 86.4%, a specificity of 98.4%, and a diagnostic efficiency of 96.5%. The method was evaluated using 144 samples from domestic and wild animals, including bats, and was found to be reliable for detecting rabies virus variants in Kazakhstan. The findings have significant implications for improving laboratory diagnostics and epidemiological monitoring of rabies in the region. The study's evidence is strong, but its generalizability may be limited to the specific geographic and host contexts examined.

title: Atypical neuroimaging in rabies encephalitis: A case report of concurrent cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in a nine-year-old patient

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human rabies is a uniformly fatal encephalitis that poses diagnostic challenges when exposure history is absent, creating uncertainty in early clinical recognition and management.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This single-patient case report describes a 9-year-old boy from Morocco who presented with fever, seizures, psychomotor agitation, hypersalivation, and hydrophobia without a reported animal exposure history.
analysis.methods: Diagnostic evaluation included brain MRI to identify encephalitic changes and a nuchal skin biopsy analyzed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction for rabies virus RNA confirmation.
analysis.main_results: MRI revealed bilateral symmetric grey matter hyperintensities in the thalami and temporal lobes consistent with rabies encephalitis and an atypical finding of extensive cerebral venous sinus thrombosis involving the right transverse and sigmoid sinuses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the MRI as demonstrating the dual diagnostic role of imaging in rabies—supporting early etiological diagnosis while simultaneously identifying a rare macrovascular complication, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This case highlights the importance of MRI in acute encephalitis for both etiological diagnosis of rabies and detection of concurrent macrovascular complications that may influence management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to a single case report with no control group, restricting generalizability and precluding causal inference; the strength of evidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a 9-year-old boy from Morocco who presented with clinical features of rabies encephalitis despite no reported animal exposure. Brain MRI showed classic bilateral thalamic and temporal lobe hyperintensities suggestive of rabies and an atypical finding of right transverse and sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Rabies virus RNA was confirmed by RT-PCR from a nuchal skin biopsy. Despite intensive care and anticoagulation, the patient died on day 9. The authors emphasize MRI’s dual diagnostic utility in rabies—identifying encephalitic changes and concurrent macrovascular complications—but the single-case design limits broader conclusions.

title: Psychological effects of rabies on the relatives of people who died from human rabies in Côte d'Ivoire between 2023 and 2025: Qualitative Observational Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The psychological impact of rabies on relatives of deceased patients remains largely unexplored, creating a knowledge gap in understanding the broader burden of human rabies beyond mortality. The study aimed to analyse the psychological effects experienced by relatives of people who died from human rabies in Côte d'Ivoire.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A single-center descriptive qualitative study was conducted from January to June 2026 among relatives of individuals who died from confirmed or suspected human rabies between 2023 and 2025, identified through the death notification register of the Anti-Rabies Center of the National Institute of Public Hygiene.
analysis.methods: Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted until data saturation was achieved, and the data were subjected to thematic analysis to explore the psychological experiences of the relatives.
analysis.main_results: Relatives reported predominant emotional responses including sadness (18/37), helplessness (15/37), anger (8/37), shock (9/37), feelings of abandonment (1/37), and guilt (7/37). After death, intrusive memories, sleep disturbances (24/37), nightmares (15/37), and avoidance of animals (11/37) were almost universally reported, suggestive of post-traumatic psychological distress and prolonged grief.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that the burden of rabies extends beyond mortality to include profound and lasting psychological suffering among relatives, with coping relying almost exclusively on prayer (28/37) and family/community support (18/37) rather than formal psychological assistance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the need to integrate culturally appropriate psychosocial support into rabies management to address the psychological suffering of affected families and strengthen awareness toward the 2030 rabies elimination goal.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The single-center, qualitative design limits generalisability, and the absence of formal psychological support reporting may reflect local service gaps rather than universal lack of access, warranting cautious interpretation of the evidence strength as moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative observational study in Côte d'Ivoire examined the psychological effects on relatives of people who died from human rabies between 2023 and 2025. Using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, the research identified predominant emotional responses such as sadness, helplessness, anger, and shock, alongside post-traumatic symptoms including intrusive memories, sleep disturbances, nightmares, and avoidance behaviors. Coping mechanisms were almost exclusively informal, relying on prayer and family/community support, with no reported formal psychological assistance. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that rabies imposes a profound and lasting psychological burden beyond mortality. They recommend integrating culturally appropriate psychosocial components into rabies management to support affected families and advance rabies elimination goals by 2030. The single-center design and qualitative approach limit generalisability, and the lack of formal support reporting may reflect local service gaps rather than universal absence.

analysis.methods: The researchers estimated the number of undiagnosed rabies deaths by dividing the number of identified rabies-related donor deaths by the total number of deceased donors and multiplying by the total number of deaths in the US. title: Temporal trends and determinants of delayed care-seeking after rabies exposure: a 27,930-patient analysis in Tianjin

analysis.research_question_and_background: Prompt care-seeking after rabies exposure is essential for effective post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). This study aimed to identify independent factors associated with care-seeking delay and to map the full PEP pathway.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We retrospectively enrolled 27,930 patients attending the rabies PEP clinic at Santan Hospital, Tianjin, between February 2022 and January 2026. Delay was defined as >12 h from exposure to registration.
analysis.methods: Multivariable logistic regression, combined with XGBoost and SHAP, identified independent factors for delay and quantified their relative importance. Restricted cubic splines examined the non-linear relationship between age and delay. Subgroup analysis assessed the stability of the association of grade III exposure with more prompt care-seeking.
analysis.main_results: The delay rate was 29.7%. Eight independent factors were identified. Adults had a 34% higher risk of delay than children (aOR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.22-1.47, P < 0.001). Grade III exposure was associated with more prompt care-seeking (aOR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.65-0.73, P < 0.001). Previous rabies vaccination (aOR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.11-1.23, P < 0.001) and inadequate wound management (aOR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.31-1.88, P < 0.001) were associated with higher delay risk. Age showed a non-linear relationship with delay risk, with adults at highest risk.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our findings suggest that adults may face the highest risk of care-seeking delay, and that improving healthcare access for adults and promoting simplified vaccination schedules may be key to improving PEP quality.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform strategies to improve healthcare access for adults and promote simplified vaccination schedules to enhance the quality of post-exposure prophylaxis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential biases in self-reported data. The evidence is moderate as it relies on observational data and does not establish causality.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed 27,930 patients in Tianjin to identify factors associated with delayed care-seeking after rabies exposure. It found that adults had a 34% higher risk of delay compared to children, and that grade III exposure was linked to more prompt care-seeking. The research highlights the importance of improving healthcare access for adults and promoting simplified vaccination schedules to enhance post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) effectiveness. The study used multivariable logistic regression, XGBoost, and SHAP to identify independent factors, while restricted cubic splines explored the non-linear relationship between age and delay. A Sankey diagram was used to map the PEP pathway. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and potential biases in self-reported data.

title: Zoonotic disease risk perceptions associated with commercial wildlife activities in Southeast Asia: A scoping review

analysis.scope_and_question: Zoonotic disease emergence is closely linked to human-wildlife interactions, particularly in commercial wildlife activities where livelihoods, conservation, and health intersect. This scoping review examines community perceptions of zoonotic disease risks associated with commercial wildlife activities and explores their implications for One Health research and practice.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Peer-reviewed studies published in English between 2000 and 2024 were identified through PubMed and Google Scholar. Eligible studies examining community perceptions of health or zoonotic disease risks associated with wildlife hunting, trade, farming, or consumption in Southeast Asia were included in the review. Data were extracted and analyzed thematically to identify patterns, knowledge gaps, and implications for research and practice.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Study findings showed partial awareness of zoonotic risks among study populations, often limited to diseases such as avian influenza and rabies. Community perceptions of zoonotic disease risk in Southeast Asia are shaped by intersecting social, economic, cultural, and livelihood factors. Awareness of zoonotic disease risks alone is often insufficient to support preventive practices when livelihood dependence, limited access to services, sociocultural beliefs, and broader structural barriers shape decision-making and behaviors.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Gaps in translating awareness into preventive practices were highlighted, driven by livelihood dependence, poverty, limited access to services and facilities, and broader structural constraints. Cultural beliefs, gender, and education also shaped risk perceptions and responses, and illegal or informal trade contexts complicated engagement and data collection.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Effective strategies to reduce zoonotic disease risk associated with commercial wildlife activities require cross-sectoral, context-sensitive approaches that integrate community perspectives into communication and services across the conservation, public health, agriculture, and veterinary sectors. Risk reduction strategies should also move beyond awareness raising to address structural barriers that limit communities’ access to relevant information and services, thereby supporting more equitable and sustainable zoonotic disease prevention in Southeast Asia.

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review explores community perceptions of zoonotic disease risks in Southeast Asia, particularly in the context of commercial wildlife activities. The review synthesizes evidence from eight studies conducted in Thailand, Indonesia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, and Myanmar, which used qualitative or mixed-methods approaches. Findings indicate that awareness of zoonotic risks, such as rabies, is often limited and does not translate into preventive practices due to factors like livelihood dependence, poverty, and structural barriers. The review emphasizes the need for cross-sectoral, context-sensitive strategies that integrate community perspectives into public health and conservation efforts. It highlights the importance of addressing structural constraints and cultural beliefs to support more equitable and sustainable disease prevention.

title: Passive Immunization Hesitancy Among Rabies-Exposed Individuals in China: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies remains a fatal disease without effective treatment once symptoms appear, and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) including passive immunization (PI) is the only life-saving intervention. Despite clinical guidelines, real-world PI utilization is suboptimal, creating a need to understand determinants of PI hesitancy among exposed individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multicenter cross-sectional questionnaire study was conducted at 12 rabies PEP clinics or emergency departments across 12 provinces in mainland China. The analysis included 585 previously unvaccinated adults with Category III rabies exposure who initially hesitated to receive or declined PI.
analysis.methods: A structured questionnaire collected sociodemographic characteristics, exposure profiles, awareness of the early protection gap, reasons for initial PI hesitancy or refusal, subsequent PI acceptance during the same encounter, and PI product selection. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with PI treatment decisions, with adjusted odds ratios (aORs) reported and reason-specific models corrected for false discovery rate using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.
analysis.main_results: Among 5068 eligible previously unvaccinated patients with Category III rabies exposure, 2866 (57%) initially hesitated to receive or declined recommended PI. Of 617 questionnaire respondents, 32 minors were excluded, leaving 585 adults for analysis. During the same clinical encounter, 320/585 adults (55%) chose to receive PI.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Awareness of the early protection gap was positively associated with PI choice (aOR 2.63, 95% CI 1.75–3.98), while head/face wounds were negatively associated (aOR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30–0.92). In reason-specific models, lack of knowledge about immediate protection increased PI uptake (aOR 2.43, 95% CI 1.62–3.68), whereas cost concerns reduced it (aOR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27–0.62).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeted education about the timing of PI protection and addressing cost barriers could improve adherence to PEP guidelines among rabies-exposed individuals in China.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is cross-sectional and restricted to adults, limiting causal inference and generalizability to minors or other settings. Self-reported hesitancy and recall bias may affect accuracy, and the analysis did not include clinical outcomes beyond PI acceptance.

analysis.summary_en: This multicenter cross-sectional study in China investigated passive immunization (PI) hesitancy among 585 previously unvaccinated adults with Category III rabies exposure who initially declined PI. Among 5068 eligible patients, 57% hesitated or refused PI, but 55% accepted PI during the same clinical encounter. Awareness of the early protection gap and higher education were positively associated with PI acceptance, while head/face wounds and cost concerns were negative predictors. The study highlights modifiable barriers—knowledge gaps and financial constraints—and suggests that targeted education and cost mitigation could improve adherence to rabies post-exposure prophylaxis guidelines.

title: Community Knowledge, Canine Seroprevalence, and the Vaccination Paradox: A One Health Assessment of Rabies in Rural and Urban Kenya

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies remains a fatal yet vaccine-preventable zoonosis, with Kenya committed to the global "Zero by 30" elimination target. analysis.study_design_and_population: An across-sectional study was conducted between August 2024 and September 2025 across Kitui County (n = 322 households) and Nairobi (n = 276 households), comprising 598 household surveys administered via Kobo Collect. Canine serum samples (n = 91) from Kitui were analyzed to measure rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies (RVNA).
analysis.methods: The study used a validated competitive ELISA (Platelia® Rabies II) to measure rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies (RVNA) against the WHO/WOAH protective threshold of ≥ 0.5 IU/ml. analysis.main_results: General community awareness of rabies was high at 92.1%, with rural Kitui residents exhibiting significantly greater awareness (98.4%) than urban Nairobi residents (84.8%; p < 0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights a vaccination paradox where high reported vaccination coverage does not necessarily correlate with actual seroprotection, suggesting a need for improved biological monitoring of immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of biological seroprotection as a more accurate metric for rabies control than administrative vaccination coverage, with implications for surveillance and intervention strategies in Kenya.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported vaccination data and a relatively small sample size of canine serum samples. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the relationship between reported vaccination coverage and actual seroprotection against rabies in rural and urban Kenya. It highlights a vaccination paradox where high reported coverage does not equate to sufficient biological immunity. The research underscores the importance of biological monitoring over administrative data for effective rabies control. The study's findings suggest that community knowledge and attitudes play a critical role in rabies prevention. However, the study's reliance on self-reported data and a limited sample size of canine serum samples may affect the strength of its conclusions. The results have implications for improving surveillance and intervention strategies in Kenya.
